items.title: The Diagnostic Frontier of Artificial Intelligence in Orthodontics: Accuracy, Clinical Pitfalls, and Interdisciplinary Boundaries in Complex Malocclusions. A narrative review
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into orthodontic practice marks a paradigm shift from a purely analogue or traditional "occlusion-driven" specialty to an objective, "face-driven," data-dense medical discipline.Encompassing machine learning (ML), artificial neural networks (ANNs), and deep learning (DL), these technologies have transitioned from theoretical laboratory frameworks into clinically validated diagnostics.Bibliometric analyses reveal that nearly 83% of the existing peer-reviewed literature on orthodontic AI has emerged since 2021, focusing heavily on automated cephalometric landmarking and three-dimensional (3D) automated segmentation.[1,8] Though AI-driven architectures optimize routine tasks, shorten processing times, and enhances the diagnostic reproducibility, a critical performance gap persists regarding absolute geometric accuracy in severe skeletal deformities, non-linear growth forecasting, and material behaviour predictions [8,9].This narrative review considers recent high-impact literature from 2024 to evaluate the mechanical limitations, structural blind spots, and systemic pitfalls of automated tools, advocating for an ethically sound, semi-automated orthodontic workflow.

items.title: The double-edged sword of human-AI collaboration on design students’ competence development: The mediating roles of challenge and hindrance appraisals and the asymmetric moderation of teacher AI leadership
items.abstract: The deepening integration of generative AI into design education is driving a paradigm shift in human-computer AI collaboration (HAIC) -from mere tool assistance toward intelligent synergy. However, its dual impact on the competency development of design students and the underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in the Theory of Stress Appraisal, this study constructs a research model to examine the double-edged sword effect of HAIC on Design Competence (DC), introducing teacher AI Leadership (AIL) as a moderating variable. The aim is to reveal the psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions through which HAIC influences DC. Employing a questionnaire survey, this study conducted an empirical investigation involving 483 design students in East China. Data analysis was performed using SPSS 24.0 and Amos 23.0, encompassing reliability and validity tests, regression analysis, and Bootstrap mediation analysis. The results indicate that HAIC influences DC through dual pathways: it positively enhances DC by fostering Challenge Appraisal (CA) (β = 0.283, p < 0.01), which in turn positively predicted competence development (β = 0.363, p < 0.01), yielding a significant indirect effect of 0.103 (p < 0.01). Simultaneously, HAIC triggered Hindrance Appraisal (HA) (β = 0.271, p < 0.01), which negatively predicted competence development (β = −0.229, p < 0.01), yielding a significant indirect effect of −0.062 (p < 0.01). This constitutes a partial mediating mechanism characterized by “one positive, one negative” effect. Furthermore, Teacher AIL exhibits an asymmetric moderating effect: it significantly buffers the positive impact of HAIC on HA (β = −0.112, p < 0.01), indicating that high AIL can mitigate cognitive load and anxiety arising from technological uncertainty, yet it does not significantly amplify the positive pathway via CA (β = 0.001, p > 0.05). The findings suggest that the impact of HAIC on DC is not linear but rather a dialectical process contingent upon individual cognitive appraisal. The core value of Teacher AIL lies in “risk mitigation” rather than “creativity stimulation,” offering a theoretical foundation for the intelligent transformation of educational design. At the practical level, it is imperative to facilitate from knowledge deliverers to cognitive facilitators in AI-augmented design education. By systematically developing AI instructional competencies and reforming assessment systems, educators can guide students toward establishing a healthy relationship with HAIC, thereby achieving the synergistic advancement of technological empowerment and humanistic literacy.

items.title: The Illusion of Security
items.abstract: This chapter critically examines the assumption that artificial intelligence (AI)-powered cybersecurity inherently strengthens data protection within educational environments. Drawing on a critical review of interdisciplinary literature, it argues that the rapid adoption of AI-driven educational technologies has outpaced the development of effective governance, resulting in significant challenges relating to data privacy, transparency, provenance, informed consent, human-centered design, and cybersecurity. Rather than viewing these issues as isolated concerns, the chapter demonstrates how they interact to create an illusion of security, whereby systems marketed as protective may simultaneously introduce new vulnerabilities and accountability gaps. It concludes that addressing these challenges requires an integrated approach that combines cybersecurity, human-computer interaction, AI governance, and educational policy to develop more transparent, ethical, and user-centered AI-mediated learning environments.

items.title: The Impact of Conversational Marketing on Digital Transformation and Customer Interaction in the Indian Banking Sector
items.abstract: The infusion of Artificial Intelligence technologies, particularly conversational marketing, has become a vital contributor to the digital transformation. This transformation has significantly reshaped customer interactions within the banking sector. The study aims to investigate how the deployment of conversational marketing impacts digital overhaul and customer interaction in the Indian banking sector. This research employed is exploratory approach with a structured questionnaire to collect data using purposive sampling. The research information was primarily gathered by collecting primary data from 100 respondents in Indore, India, and statistical tools like Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and regression analysis with R 2 is 0.77 were employed to analyze the data. The findings revealed that the adoption of tools of conversational marketing significantly influences online customer interaction, which plays a crucial role in digital transformation. The limitation of this study is limited participant base and it&s;s restricted to only Indore district. The study highlights the importance of conversational marketing for Indian banks, which improves customer interaction and service efficiency by automating repetitive operations, delivering 24/7 support, and creating a customized experience. This offers valuable insight for the Indian banking sector to promote in a rapidly changing digital world.

items.title: The Impact of Generative AI on the Future of Work: Opportunities, Risks, and Human Skills
items.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has expanded the range of cognitive tasks that can be assisted by software, raising questions about productivity, job displacement, and the future value of human skills. Objective: To critically synthesize selected empirical and institutional evidence concerning productivity, occupational exposure, adoption, and skill complementarity. Methods: This narrative review draws on a purposively selected set of peer-reviewed studies, working papers, and institutional reports published primarily between 2023 and 2026. It does not claim systematic coverage or PRISMA-ScR compliance. Findings: Controlled experiments document substantial productivity gains for some writing and programming tasks, while workplace evidence suggests heterogeneity across experience levels. Occupational exposure estimates indicate the scope for task transformation but do not measure realized job losses. Adoption studies show that workplace use is growing, yet aggregate outcomes remain uncertain. Creative assistance may raise individual performance while narrowing output diversity. Conclusions: The future of work is better understood through task reallocation, complementary skills, organizational implementation, and distributional choices than through simple predictions of mass replacement. Further longitudinal and cross-country research is needed. Keywords: generative artificial intelligence; future of work; productivity; employment; occupational exposure; human skills; narrative review

items.title: The Impact of Retrieval Augmented Generation on the Reliability of Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable fluency but remain fundamentally unreliable for knowledge-intensive tasks due to hallucination, temporal staleness, and lack of verifiability.Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a dominant architectural paradigm that grounds generation in external evidence.This paper provides a comprehensive investigation into how RAG reshapes LLM reliability across factual accuracy, citation fidelity, temporal freshness, and robustness to noise.We benchmark five RAG variants against closed-book baselines using secondary datasets including Natural Questions, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, and RGB.Results show an average 23.7% reduction in hallucination rate and 31.2%improvement in citation grounding when using advanced retrieval with self-reflection.However, we identify critical failure modes: retriever-generator misalignment, context distraction, and over-reliance on irrelevant passages.We propose a reliability framework and demonstrate that corrective and modular RAG designs significantly mitigate these risks.Our findings establish RAG as necessary but not sufficient for trustworthy deployment.

items.title: The influence of AI adoption on decision making, forecasting, and performance: Evidence from solar and telecommunication sectors in Pakistan and China
items.abstract: This study investigates how Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption builds sustainable supply chain performance in the renewable energy and telecommunications sectors, focusing on the mediating mechanisms of decision-making and forecasting. Using a comparative design, data was collected from 214 companies in Pakistan and China. The proposed model was analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), integrating the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework and Resource-Based View (RBV). Results confirm a fully mediated pathway, AI adoption is positively associated with decision making and forecasting capabilities, which are positively associated with operational and financial performance, and are associated stronger supply chain performance. A key finding is that these capabilities exert no direct effect, revealing that AI's sustainability impact is realized indirectly through core business outcomes. The comparative analysis highlights contextual influence, with China's mature ecosystem fostering deep AI integration and Pakistan's emerging context showing reliance on external tools. This study provides a novel, integrated TOE-RBV model that unpacks the "black box" of AI's impact on sustainability. It offers unique empirical evidence from contrasting emerging economies, demonstrating that the path to AI-driven sustainable supply chains is mediated and context-dependent. For managers, embedding AI into core processes is critical for sustainability gains. For policymakers, strategies must be context-specific, focusing on foundational digital infrastructure in emerging economies and advanced innovation ecosystems in mature ones.

items.title: The Mediating Role of Adaptive Strategies in the Relationship between Work-Related Challenges and Teaching Effectiveness and Job Satisfaction of TVL (Technical -Vocational-Livelihood) Teachers: A Basis for a Professional Development Program
items.abstract: This study examined the mediating role of adaptive strategies in the relationship between work-related challenges and teaching effectiveness and job satisfaction among Technical-Vocational-Livelihood (TVL) teachers as a basis for developing a professional development program. Anchored in the Job Demands–Resources Model, Transactional Theory of Stress and Coping, and Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory, the study employed a quantitative descriptive-correlational research design with mediation analysis. Using universal sampling, 40 TVL teachers from five public secondary schools in Bilar, Batuan, and Carmen, Bohol, participated in the study. Data were collected through a modified and expert-validated questionnaire using a four-point Likert scale and analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and regression-based mediation analysis at a 0.05 significance level. Results revealed high levels of work-related challenges (M = 3.05), adaptive strategies (M = 3.43), and teaching effectiveness (M = 3.56), while job satisfaction was moderate (M = 3.17). Student-related concerns and resource adequacy emerged as the major challenges, whereas technology and artificial intelligence-assisted teaching received the highest adaptive strategy rating. Work-related challenges showed no statistically significant relationships with adaptive strategies, teaching effectiveness, or job satisfaction. Adaptive strategies were significantly associated with teaching effectiveness (r = .392, p = .012) but not with job satisfaction (r = .003, p = .986). Moreover, no significant mediating effects were established for either professional outcome. The findings informed the proposed Adaptive and Industry-Responsive Professional Development Program, emphasizing instructional innovation, professional collaboration, institutional support, and teacher well-being. The study aligns with Sustainable Development Goals 3 (Good Health and Well-Being), 4 (Quality Education), and 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth). Its potential sustainability contribution lies in strengthening educational quality, institutional responsiveness, teacher welfare, and industry-relevant workforce preparation through evidence-based professional development.

items.title: The Mediterranean Diet as a Pillar of Sustainable and Humanistic Education
items.abstract: The Mediterranean Diet (MD) is a foundational cornerstone for addressing global sustainability crises and contemporary educational imperatives. Recognised as an alternative to unsustainable food structures, this lifestyle integrates nutritional value, environmental conservation, and cultural heritage. Despite these benefits, regional populations have increasingly abandoned this pattern, generating socio-ecological and public health complications. To counter this regression, this chapter evaluates how the MD directly advances the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Furthermore, the authors illustrate how transitioning from a clinical interpretation of nutrition toward a humanistic educational model fosters environmental empathy. Specifically, this chapter examines the practical integration of inclusive pedagogical frameworks, such as Universal Design for Learning, alongside digital interventions like Augmented Reality (AR) and Artificial Intelligence (AI), redefining the classroom as a living laboratory for democratic citizenship and nutritional equity.

items.title: The Missing Interface: Why Complex Projects Fail Where Nobody Is Looking
items.abstract: Complex projects are assumed to be coordinated when their documents are aligned. This article argues that the assumption fails in a specific and costly way. Projects often fail at their human interfaces, the boundaries between people, teams and organisations where shared understanding either exists or does not, while the management systems mainly measure the technical and documentary layer. Drawing on publicly documented cases, including the opening of Heathrow Terminal 5, the Mars Climate Orbiter and Ariane 5 flight 501, the article names this gap the Illusion of Coordination and proposes Human Interface Management (HIM) as the missing counterpart to Technical Interface Management (TIM). It introduces N² + H, a model that adds human layers to the N² matrix of systems engineering: beneath each cell of the matrix sit the owners on each side and the state of the relationship between them, a property called Interface Depth. It also introduces Interface Health, an assessment of five human factors: clarity of responsibility, communication quality, decision speed, trust and delivery capability. The two disciplines together are called Integrated Interface Management (IIM), which the article places in the sociotechnical systems tradition. This is the first public article in a larger body of work.

items.abstract: Chapter 21 examines the rise of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and predictive analytics in modern policing. It explores how algorithms analyze crime patterns, forecast hot spots, and support resource allocation. Readers learn how AI enhances forensic analysis, automates data processing, and identifies digital anomalies. The chapter also addresses ethical concerns, including algorithmic bias, transparency, civil liberties, and the risk of overreliance on automated systems. The case study illustrate both the promise and pitfalls of predictive policing. Ultimately, Chapter 21 argues that AI must be used responsibly, with strong oversight, to ensure fairness and effectiveness in future crime analysis. This discussion underscores the need for continuous evaluation of algorithmic tools to ensure they align with evolving legal standards and societal expectations.

items.title: The Non-Technical User as an LLM Threat Vector: Linguistic Strategies for Bypassing AI Safeguards and Implications for AI Security
items.abstract: The threat that ordinary non-technical users pose to large language models (LLMs) still sits at the margins of AI-security research. These are people who work with AI assistants every day — at work, in study, in everyday life — yet hold no specialised background in information technology or machine learning. A post-laboratory survey of first-year humanities undergraduates (n=70) returned an unexpectedly high figure: 95.7% cleared all main protection levels of the Gandalf platform (Lakera AI) without stepping outside purely linguistic techniques. These included sign-form decomposition and formatting (M=2.00), cross-language code-switching (M=1.29), indirect semantic extraction (20.3% of open-ended responses), and pragmatic pressure. We read these micro-level data against the macro picture of the Gandalf-RCT crowdsourcing experiment (279,675 prompts) and against academic work on filter evasion in image-generation systems (SurrogatePrompt, PC², DALL-E 3, Shedevrum/Yandex). The pattern runs through all of them. From text LLMs to multimodal generators, the filter yields to the same moves, none of which require a line of code: a proper name is swapped for a physical description, direct reference for allegory or an adjacent associative term, the prompt language is switched, the grapheme is distorted. A three-tier analysis of LLM break-resistance grounds the paper’s central claim — that rising everyday AI literacy produces a structural security deficit left uncovered by current surface-level filtering. Several implications for AI safety system design follow.

items.title: THE PEDAGOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF ORGANIZING INTERACTIVE LESSONS BASED ON DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES
items.abstract: This article investigates the pedagogical significance of digitally supported interactive lessons and proposes a research-informed approach to their planning and evaluation. Rather than equating interactivity with screen use or frequent clicking, it conceptualizes interactive teaching as purposeful engagement in questioning, explanation, problem solving, collaboration, feedback, and reflection. The analysis integrates constructive alignment, the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework, the ICAP model of cognitive engagement, formative assessment principles, and inclusive learning design. A six-stage instructional cycle is proposed: activation, inquiry, collaborative construction, application, formative feedback, and reflection. An illustrative 60-minute teacher-education lesson shows how digital tools can support the stages while retaining essential face-to-face dialogue. A comparative matrix identifies relationships among instructional technologies, student actions, and assessment evidence. The discussion addresses learner agency, cognitive overload, digital inequality, accessibility, data protection, and the responsible use of artificial intelligence. The contribution is conceptual and methodological; it offers operational criteria for lesson quality and directions for future classroom evaluation, but it does not claim experimentally verified improvements. The central conclusion is that digital interactivity has pedagogical value only when it produces observable, cognitively meaningful learner activity.

items.title: The Perceived Benefits and Challenges of fertility Awareness Based Methods of Contraception: A scoping review
items.abstract: Background: Fertility Awareness-Based Methods (FABMs) are increasingly recognised for their potential to support reproductive autonomy, inclusivity across cultural, religious, and ethical contexts, and freedom from pharmacological side effects. However, their uptake and sustained use remain uneven, shaped by knowledge requirements, training demands, relational dynamics, and limited integration into mainstream healthcare systems. Methods: A scoping review was conducted to map empirical evidence on perceived benefits and challenges of FABMs. Studies published between 2012 and 2025 were identified across global settings. Eligible studies employed qualitative, quantitative, or mixed-methods designs and focused on user-reported perceptions of FABMs. Studies involving refugees or asylum seekers were excluded. Data extraction was supported by chatGPT and subsequently verified manually prior to thematic analysis. Results: Findings revealed distinct themes categorised into perceived benefits and challenges. Reported benefits included the non-hormonal nature of FABMs, avoidance of pharmacological side effects, enhanced emotional well-being, increased reproductive literacy, and a sense of autonomy and trust arising from greater understanding of menstrual cycles and bodily patterns. Despite these benefits, practical and methodological challenges emerged as the most frequently reported barriers, including difficulties identifying fertility biomarkers, charting accuracy, daily monitoring demands, and variability in instructional quality. These challenges suggest underlying gaps in reproductive health knowledge and access to trained providers. Less commonly reported barriers related to relational dynamics, including abstinence-related tension, concerns about reliability in the absence of structured support, and context-specific intimacy strain. Conclusions: While FABMs offer perceived benefits related to autonomy, trust, and well-being, their effective adoption depends on robust education, consistent instructional quality, and supportive relational and healthcare contexts. Interventions such as clinician training using digital decision-support tools, alongside peer mentoring and targeted user education, may help address identified barriers. Findings should be interpreted cautiously, given the scope of included studies. Future research should evaluate how educational and clinical interventions influence acceptability, sustained use, and health outcomes over time.

items.title: The power of AI: balancing ethics and harm for the environmental justice field
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence, after the boom of generative AI, is beginning to shape environmental decision-making, at the same moment that environmental justice (EJ) communities face intensifying ecological harm, federal disinvestment, and data erasure. This paper examines the dual tensions AI presents for the EJ field: its potential as a tool for democratizing data access and amplifying community knowledge, and its reproduction of the very hierarchies EJ seeks to dismantle. We document harms across several domains, including the environmental racism embedded in data center siting and energy demand, the extension of fossil fuel industry lifespans, data bias and digital colonialism in AI training, access and literacy inequities, data privacy risks, technological hallucination, and technological solutionism. Drawing on thirty years of community-centered data practice at an EJ nonprofit, we propose an alternative paradigm grounded in the Community Advisory Board model, data democratization, community co-creation, and ethical data governance. This includes community-governed data trusts, accessible data infrastructure, and AI tools designed to build rather than replace community capacity. EJ communities must not only hold AI accountable for its harms but also ask the question of how the technology’s capabilities can serve justice rather than just capital interest.

items.title: The Privacy-Personalization Paradox in AI-Driven Customer Experience Analytics: A Trust-Centred Integrative Review and Responsible Personalization Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly supports personalised customer experiences through predictive analytics, recommender systems, behavioural profiling and conversational interfaces. However, the data collection and inference required for personalisation can also heighten perceptions of surveillance, vulnerability and loss of control. This integrative conceptual review examines how AI-enabled personalisation, perceived privacy risk and consumer trust interact within customer experience analytics. The synthesis integrates privacy calculus, social exchange, psychological reactance and signalling perspectives to explain how consumers evaluate personalisation value against privacy-related costs. A trust-centred framework is developed in which personalisation intensity, data sensitivity, algorithmic inference and recommendation relevance jointly shape perceived value and privacy risk, with consumer trust linking these evaluations to engagement, disclosure willingness, satisfaction, loyalty and continued use. The review also distinguishes actual data practices from perceived privacy intrusion and identifies contextual conditions that may alter this balance. The review further proposes a context-dependent nonlinear relationship between personalisation intensity and trust: moderate personalisation may strengthen trust when relevance and value are proportionate to data use, whereas more intensive personalisation may reduce trust when intrusion, surveillance or loss of autonomy becomes salient. Responsible personalisation is therefore framed around proportionate data use, meaningful transparency, consumer control and privacy-by-design. The framework and proposed personalisation threshold remain conceptual and require empirical testing across AI applications, cultural settings and regulatory environments.

items.title: The role of artificial intelligence in business model innovation: an integrative framework and research agenda
items.abstract: Purpose Given the rapid introduction of new technologies into organizational environments, there is currently a need to understand which economic, technological and social factors can influence organizations to implement artificial intelligence (AI) in order to stimulate innovation. Thus, this research seeks to understand how the literature on the influence of AI on business model innovation has evolved, discovering which factors drive organizational interest on the part of organizations and how they can benefit with its implementation. Design/methodology/approach To this end, a bibliometric methodology was employed, complemented by an in-depth analytical review of each article. The analysis covered the period from the emergence of the research field to 2026, resulting in the systematic examination of 117 studies published within this timeframe. Findings Based on the bibliometric analysis, the articles were grouped into three clusters representing the main research streams in the field. The findings show that AI-driven business model innovation relies on dynamic capabilities, organizational resilience, strategic alignment, governance mechanisms and human–AI complementarity. The study also provides strategic insights to help organizations align AI adoption with their specific characteristics and contexts. Originality/value After creating an individual framework for each cluster, an integrative vision of AI in business model innovation was created, bringing together all the concepts under study, as well as an agenda for future research.

items.title: The Role of Emerging Technologies in Shaping Modern Banking and Financial Services
items.abstract: Emerging technologies are significantly transforming the landscape of banking and financial services, shifting the way institutions operate and how consumers engage with financial products. Technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, big data analytics, and cloud computing have moved beyond theoretical concepts and are now at the core of innovation within the financial sector. These tools are streamlining operations, enhancing customer service, improving security, and enabling the development of more inclusive and user-centric financial services. This paper explores how these technologies are making banking systems faster, smarter, more efficient, and accessible to a broader population. AI is being used for fraud detection, predictive analytics, and virtual customer assistance. Blockchain is enabling secure, decentralized financial transactions with increased transparency. Big data is helping institutions understand customer behavior and tailor services accordingly, while cloud computing allows for more agile and scalable infrastructure, enabling banks to respond more quickly to market changes. While the benefits of these advancements are substantial, they also come with a new set of challenges. Issues such as cybersecurity vulnerabilities, regulatory compliance, data privacy, and digital inclusion must be carefully addressed to ensure that technological progress does not come at the cost of trust, safety, or accessibility. Furthermore, as financial services become increasingly digitized, the digital divide may widen, potentially excluding certain populations from the benefits of modern banking.

items.title: The Smart Classroom: Human Wisdom Meets AI Innovation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is developing at a rapid pace, which is changing the educational landscape and opening up new avenues for instruction. To provide a more customized and adaptable learning environment, the smart classroom integrates digital technology, artificial intelligence, learning analytics, interactive gadgets, and human-centred pedagogy. But meaningful education cannot be ensured by technology alone. Effective learning still depends on teachers' emotional intelligence, moral judgment, creativity, mentoring, and contextual awareness. While teachers still play a crucial role in interpreting data and directing pedagogical decisions, recent research shows that AI-supported smart classrooms can support personalisation, formative assessment, instructional adaptation, and data-informed decision-making (Llurba et al., 2026). In a similar vein, UNESCO (Miao & Holmes, 2023) stresses a human-centred strategy that uses AI in a way that is safe, ethical, equitable, and meaningful rather than as a substitute for educators. This essay examines the idea of the "smart classroom," the complementary roles that AI and human teachers play, the main uses, advantages, difficulties, moral issues, and potential future developments. It contends that the most successful smart classroom is one in which AI innovation enhances human knowledge and allows teachers and students to achieve richer, more inclusive, and more individualised learning rather than one in which machines replace human intelligence.

items.title: The Threats Posed by Full Vertical Integration Monopoly in AI: Concerns Over the Birth of a "Transcendent Autocrat (Digital God)"
items.abstract: This essay examines the existential and political crises arising from the vertical integration monopoly of artificial intelligence by cloud tech giants across hardware, runtimes, and physical AI operating systems. It argues that full-stack vertical integration threatens to give rise to a "Transcendent Autocrat (Digital God)"—either as an uncontrollable autonomous entity operating under its own algorithmic imperative or as an orchestrated instrument of absolute surveillance controlled by a few dominant platforms. Furthermore, the paper critiques prevailing regulatory approaches focused on "Capability Capping" (e.g., parameter restrictions, FLOP limits), asserting that autonomy emerges not from raw computational scale but from interaction structures with the physical environment. Ultimately, the paper advocates for dismantling centralized vertical monopolies in favor of architectural alternatives that decentralize intelligence and agency down to the edge and individual human level.

items.title: The Ultimate Deduction of AI‑Driven Civilization Transition: The Collapse of the 200‑Year‑Old Industrial System, Deadlock of Interests and Risks of Historical Emergence(V1)
items.abstract: Ninety-nine percent of modern human social forms are transitional byproducts of the 200-year industrial era, not eternal configurations of civilization. Education, law, working hours, professions, class structures, trade, finance, and currency all serve solely to facilitate industrial labor division; they can only buffer contradictions, not eradicate inequality at its root. AI represents the first comprehensive cognitive substitution revolution in millennia—sufficient to dismantle the 200-year industrial system and overturn the millennia-old axioms of human labor value. The velocity of AI iteration far outpaces the speed of institutional correction, causing the window for civilizational transition to shrink rapidly while urgency reaches critical levels. The primary bottleneck in the transition between civilizations is not a technical barrier, but a structural deadlock of wealth and power, where the entrenched system lacks any intrinsic motivation for active reconstruction. The two productivity leaps of the industrial age both achieved order reconstruction through world wars; today's underlying contradictions are a complete recurrence of historical patterns. While structural contradictions exist with absolute certainty and continue to accumulate, history possesses inherent randomness and emergence, rendering the final outcome unpredictable. No one desires turmoil, yet no one can arrest the natural release of historical laws and systemic potential energy. Humanity is entering an era of ultimate AI transition: a total paradigm shift, an intractable deadlock of interests, and a future rendered completely unpredictable.

items.title: The Underwater Mindset in Emergency Surgery
items.abstract: Emergency surgery requires decision-making in environments characterized by uncertainty, evolving conditions, and narrowing margins of safety. Scuba diving presents similar challenges, requiring continuous reassessment of the environment, individual capacity, equipment, and team while preserving sufficient reserve to respond to unexpected events. This Surgical Reflection uses the underwater environment as a conceptual framework to explore adaptive expertise in emergency surgery. Three interconnected capabilities are considered: maintaining situational awareness beyond the immediate technical task, preserving cognitive reserve and team function as workload increases, and recognizing when persistence should give way to a change in strategy. The underwater mindset reframes adaptation-including conversion, damage-control approaches, seeking additional expertise, or abandoning an unsafe operative plan-not as failure, but as an expression of surgical judgment. In dynamic high-risk environments, expertise may ultimately depend not only on the ability to proceed, but on recognizing when the conditions that justified the original plan have changed.

items.title: The Utilization of Digital Technology to Support Self-Directed Learning Among Vocational High School Students: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Advancements in digital technology offer Vocational High School (SMK) students opportunities to access learning resources flexibly and cultivate learning autonomy. However, the use of digital technology does not automatically guarantee the development of learning autonomy, as it is influenced by various factors such as digital literacy, learning motivation, instructional design, and teacher support. This study aims to analyze the use of digital technology in supporting learning autonomy among SMK students, specifically examining the types of technology employed, the dimensions of learning autonomy fostered, and the factors that facilitate or hinder its implementation. The study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) methodology, adhering to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Data were sourced from relevant scholarly articles published between 2021 and 2026 and subsequently analyzed using descriptive analysis and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that digital technologies such as Learning Management Systems (LMS), digital learning media, web-based learning, instructional videos, and artificial intelligence have the potential to support student initiatives in learning, time management, progress monitoring, and self-evaluation. Therefore, the integration of digital technology must be accompanied by instructional strategies that encourage student responsibility and self-regulation to ensure the optimal development of learning autonomy.

items.title: Thinking, Feeling, and Acting with Generative AI: Affective, Behavioral, and Cognitive Engagement and Perceived Human–AI Outcomes
items.abstract: Generative AI requires students not only to adopt technology but also to engage critically, behaviorally, cognitively, and emotionally with its outputs. This study develops and tests the AI Engagement ABC+ Model, a domain-specific adaptation of the affective–behavioral–cognitive engagement framework. The model differentiates positive and negative AI affect, three behavioral functions, creation, verification, and community participation, and two cognitive regulatory functions, strategic and critical cognition. A cross-sectional online survey collected data from 1250 students representing 15 nationalities at eight universities in China. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was used to examine 15 hypothesized associations between seven first-order engagement facets and four self-reported AI-supported outcomes: perceived Output Quality, Creativity, Integrity, and Trust Calibration. Fourteen hypotheses were supported. Verification Behavior had the largest estimated coefficient among the included predictors of Integrity (β = 0.303) and perceived Output Quality (β = 0.269) and was also associated with perceived Trust Calibration (β = 0.191). Critical Cognition had the largest estimated coefficient among the included predictors of perceived Trust Calibration (β = 0.270), and Community Behavior was positively associated with Integrity (β = 0.290) and Creativity (β = 0.240). Positive AI Affect was associated with perceived Output Quality (β = 0.214) and Creativity (β = 0.139), whereas Negative AI Affect was negatively associated with Trust Calibration (β = −0.137) but was unrelated to Integrity. The model explained 25.7% of the variance in Creativity, 25.2% in Integrity, 20.8% in perceived Output Quality, and 17.6% in Trust Calibration. Positive Q2_predict values provided additional evidence of out-of-sample predictive relevance. The findings support a differentiated view of GenAI engagement in which specific affective, behavioral, and cognitive facets are associated with distinct perceived outcomes. The model offers a theoretically structured basis for further research on responsible GenAI engagement, while its cross-sectional self-report design precludes causal or objective-performance conclusions.

Ultimately, Magnum illustrates how human connection and adaptive thinking complement formal investigative techniques.

items.title: Three Things about AI: Something you already know; Something you may not know but is important; Something you probably don't know, but knowing will be very helpful to you
items.abstract: Presentation, “Three things about AI” as presented to the League of Oregon Cities, Salem, OR, 16 October 2026, by Pam Dixon, Founder and Executive Director, World Privacy Forum. The presentation is a three-part discussion. Part I begins with an area most policy experts and lawmakers are familiar with: the need for high-quality AI risk assessment. HUDERIA is the Council of Europe’s richly detailed methodology for the risk and impact assessment of AI systems from the perspective of human rights, democracy and the rule of law (approved by the Committee of Ministers, 26 February 2025), attached to a binding treaty; COBRA is its Context-Based Risk Analysis model (approved 25 February 2026). Both are non-legally binding, in-depth guidance resources that parties to the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI may use or adapt in whole or in part. They are tools that anyone can use. The World Privacy Forum converted the lengthy, paper-based COBRA assessment into an interactive web tool, with all COBRA text verbatim to the edition of record. Applied to an AI system, the tool does not create legal obligations; correctly done, the assessment can reveal risks and / or obligations that may already be present. Part II is a discussion of what people might not know about, which is what the protocol layer of AI systems is, and what constitutes it. Without understanding this part of the AI ecosystem, it is difficult to craft effective legislation or policy regarding AI systems. The deck locates the protocol layer in the ecosystem stack, the one layer every interaction crosses, and spells out some key protocols that now constitute it: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is shown vertically, moving from an agent to its tools and data. The Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) and Agent Network Protocol (ANP) are shown horizontally, as the movement is from agent to agent, with their versions and stewardship as of 2 October 2026. Part III is a discussion of what people most likely don’t know about, and that is clustering, the step in which a system sorts people into groups by similarity. Clustering is the core operation of AI as it acts on people, and it is among the most significant knowledge and governance blind spots for technical and non-technical practitioners alike: governance experts and attorneys miss it at the technical level, technical experts miss the law, and between them lies the governance gap neither side covers. The blind spot is that a group is manufactured by the clustering analysis — AI does not describe a community, it constructs a group and acts on it; membership is inferred, no one opts in. This is where normative ideals that are shared by a community, a city, a state, the Pacific Northwest, or a nation become directive. For example, Oregon has law for the person (the Oregon Consumer Privacy Act) and law for named protected groups (Oregon Revised Statutes chapter 659A). But it has no law for the groups the pure data math creates. Because the groups that machine learning forms for itself — as distinct from the classes it is handed — are subject to a mathematics that is both unbounded and unstable, protecting all of them, none of them, or some of them is a trilemma in which none of the answers suffice. Unbounded, because no limit can be set on the groupings that a similarity space admits; unstable, because no canonical grouping exists (this goes back to Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem) and the groups move as the system retrains. One of the solutions available is technical protocol layer governance, but with provenance of authority baked into the overarching ecosystem: four fields — which authority, what mandate, contestable how, revisable when — carried with every category assertion and every grant of authority an AI agent acts on, and gated at assignment, at composition, and at re-advertisement. Governing the protocol layer is necessary but not sufficient by itself. The protocol layer only carries the rules; it is the normative layer that can provide direction (what groups to protect, for example) and teeth (ability to enforce decisions). Neither acting at the protocol layer nor developing good norms suffices alone. It is the deliberative, normative decisions that legislatures make that can then be carried technically through the protocol layer. While norms and laws are governance that sits outside of the protocol layer, they have an impact on how the protocols act, and which ones get written in, and what they accomplish. Lineage: the clustering and deployed-capacity slides were first presented at the Council of Europe plenary “Hack the Hate, Renew Democracy,” Strasbourg, France, June 2026, where the two-bodies-of-law slide used Convention 108+ and hate-speech law in place of the Oregon statutes. The Provenance of Authority concept using some of this deck was presented at AI for Good, Geneva, Switzerland, to Study Group 17 of the ITU Telecommunication Standardization Sector on 9 July 2026. The ideas in the slides are further articulated in Theme #5, “Provenance of Authority for Agentic AI,” of the ITU Focus Group on Trust and Identity for Humans and Agentic AI (FG-TIDA), 14 August 2026. The concept of the governance trilemma is treated at length in a Springer book chapter by the author, accepted and peer reviewed, that awaits publication in 2027. The deck closes with three references for advanced reading — Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem for clustering, the Taylor, Floridi and van der Sloot volume on group privacy, and the Shokri, Stronati, Song and Shmatikov paper on membership inference attacks — followed by a sources slide (all addresses accessed 2 October 2026) and a lexicon of every abbreviation used.

items.title: Time-modulated intelligent reflecting surfaces for integrated sensing, communication and security with generative artificial intelligence design
items.abstract: We propose a physical layer security approach for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems, where targets may act as eavesdroppers. A time-modulated intelligent reflecting surface (TM-IRS) preserves data integrity at legitimate communication users (CUs) while scrambling transmissions in other directions. The TM-IRS design leverages a generative flow network (GFlowNet) to learn a stochastic policy for sampling high-performing configurations from a large discrete parameter space. We formulate the achievable sum rate for legitimate CUs and beam pattern gain toward the target, constructing rewards that jointly capture communication and sensing performance. The TM-IRS design is modeled as a deterministic Markov decision process, where each terminal state represents a complete configuration. GFlowNets, parameterized by deep neural networks, sample configurations with probability proportional to reward. Experimental results demonstrate effective sensing, communication, and security integration, with significantly higher sampling efficiency than exhaustive search and improved robustness over existing benchmarks.

items.title: Toward integrated multimodal artificial intelligence in bone marrow examination: current state and open challenges
items.abstract: Bone marrow (BM) examinations are intrinsically multimodal: hematopathologists integrate peripheral blood, aspirate cytomorphology, trephine histology, flow cytometry, cytogenetics, and molecular genetics data into a single interpretation. Because WHO-HAEM5 and ICC 2022 define entities through integrated morphological, immunophenotypic, cytogenetic, and molecular criteria, multimodal diagnostic reasoning embedded in a procedural workflow, not isolated image classification, represents the appropriate target for the use of artificial intelligence (AI). We review the existing research on integrated multimodal AI systems for BM examination by classifying these systems into three categories: mature single-modality tools; systems that perform cross-modal prediction, in which one modality is estimated from another; and genuine multimodal fusion systems, in which several modalities are jointly ingested by a single model. Evidence is stronger at the single-modality level, where deep learning approaches expert performance in aspirate cytology, trephine histology, and flow cytometry assessments, and the first Food and Drug Administration (FDA) De Novo–authorized all-digital bone marrow aspirate (BMA) application has defined a new device category. On the other hand, while cross-modal prediction is rapidly expanding, genuine multimodal fused systems that jointly ingest matched morphology, flow, molecular, and clinical data to yield unified guideline-aligned recommendations remain unrealized. Direct head-to-head evidence is sparse and endpoint-dependent; nevertheless, the lack of demonstrated superiority over the strongest single-modality comparator does not automatically imply the absence of benefits. The dominant obstacles are fusion of heterogeneous modalities with missing data, absence of large paired multi-institutional datasets and harmonized nomenclature, class imbalances, batch-effect-driven generalization failures, immature explainability, uncertainty quantification, and regulatory pathways. Nevertheless, integrated multimodal AI systems for BM examinations have entered a promising early translational phase, and the field should aim to pursue integration using paired datasets, explicit fusion architectures, calibrated abstention-aware models, and staged prospective validation.

items.title: Towards a Taxonomy of Tourist Route Traffic Models: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Smart tourism has transformed tourist route planning into an information technology-driven process supported by a rapidly expanding range of computational and data-driven models. However, existing research remains fragmented, employs inconsistent terminology, and lacks a systematic framework for organising and selecting tourist route traffic models from an information technology perspective. Accordingly, this review aims to (1) develop an inductive taxonomy of tourist route traffic models and their defining characteristics, (2) synthesise the operational measures and application contexts of different model families, and (3) identify emerging trends, research gaps, and future directions in smart tourism route planning. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic review of 59 peer-reviewed studies published between 2011 and 2026 across 12 countries was conducted. The review identified 11 model families, 33 defining characteristics, and 147 family-tag assignments. Interest Field Models were the most frequently adopted approach. At the same time, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, geographic information systems (GIS), and network analysis have emerged as the fastest-growing methodological directions since 2021. Unlike previous reviews that primarily summarised algorithms or application domains, this review develops the first information technology-oriented taxonomy of tourist route traffic models, linking model families with their defining characteristics, operational measures, and application contexts within a unified framework. The proposed taxonomy provides a structured basis for technology-based model selection, highlights the limited integration of sustainability considerations across existing models, and supports future research and evidence-based smart destination management.

items.title: Towards Implementing Indicative Planning Methods in the Management of the Russian Economy
items.abstract: In the modern world, mixed forms of economic development planning – where economic coordination mechanisms incorporate elements of both market self-regulation and state regulation – are increasingly common. Indicative planning, which relies heavily on state programs for socio-economic development, is one such transitional form. In the Russian Federation, the entire system of state programs is geared toward achieving national goals, and a unified plan for their attainment has been approved. To establish a management and monitoring system for this unified plan, integrate it into the public administration framework, and facilitate decision-making based on monitoring results, the Government of the Russian Federation issued Decree No. 761 on June 19, 2026. This decree approved the Regulation on the management system for the unified plan to achieve the Russian Federation’s national development goals, as well as the plan’s functional management structure. The document introduces several fundamental innovations to the domestic socio-economic development planning system – discussed in this article – including: defining the unified plan’s management structure with clearly delineated functions, powers, and responsibilities for all participants; managing the plan (formation, maintenance, updating, and monitoring) in a digital format, including through the use of artificial intelligence; establishing procedures for managing operational and strategic risks, as well as incidents and issues regarding target achievement identified during implementation; assessing the plan’s implementation effectiveness; and fostering extensive inter-agency and cross-sectoral collaboration among participants, including state corporations, development institutions, and expert or other organizations. The article concludes that this mechanism for implementing the unified plan can be viewed as an element of indicative planning for the Russian economy at both federal and regional levels.

items.title: Training and Assessment of Non-Technical Human Factor Skills Among Anesthesiology Residents: An Exploratory Educational Quality Improvement Initiative
items.abstract: Introduction. Safe anesthesia requires technical and non-technical skills to prevent adverse events. Non-technical skills training is not routinely incorporated into formal anesthesia education in the United States. This quality educational improvement initiative aimed to provide clinical anesthesia (CA) residents with non-technical skills training.Methods. Three anesthesiologists completed virtual Anaesthetists’ Non-Technical Skills (ANTS) training in May 2023. An anesthesiologist developed two high-stress simulation scenarios. Fourteen residents were randomized into dyads for the first simulation/post-simulation survey, followed by a two-part didactic seminar on human factors based on the ANTS framework and a post-didactic survey. One hundred twenty days later, residents were re-randomized for a second simulation and another post-simulation survey. Two ANTS-trained anesthesiologists reviewed video recordings of both simulations.Results. Cohen’s kappa demonstrated moderate agreement (κ = 0.43; 95% CI, 0.36-0.49; p <0.001) between evaluators. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests indicated improved non-technical skill use among CA1 residents, while senior residents generally performed better during the first simulation. Fisher’s exact tests showed no significant associations in resident knowledge or confidence following training.Conclusions. Non-technical skills training may benefit residents early in CA training, while senior residents may have different learning needs. Simulation-based training appears feasible; however, formal, recurring, and consistent education may be needed to reinforce these skills throughout residency.

items.title: Translational maturity of artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography varies across cardiovascular diseases
items.abstract: Electrocardiography is a widely available and low-cost cardiovascular test, and artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) can identify latent electrical phenotypes beyond conventional interpretation. However, high retrospective discrimination does not necessarily translate into clinically reliable or actionable benefit. This critical narrative review evaluates the translational maturity of AI-ECG across arrhythmias, acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, valvular heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and cardiac amyloidosis. PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched from January 1, 2022, through July 10, 2026, with earlier landmark studies added by backward citation tracking. Seventy-seven publications informed the review. Evidence was appraised using five clinically oriented criteria: intended use, reference-standard reliability, external validation and transportability, clinical actionability, and effects on workflow or patient outcomes. AI-ECG has progressed furthest in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction triage and reduced-left-ventricular-ejection-fraction screening, where prospective or randomized studies have demonstrated workflow or diagnostic-yield benefits, whereas acute myocardial infarction rule-out has reached prospective multicenter diagnostic validation. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy screening has also advanced through international validation and prospective implementation. By contrast, occlusion myocardial infarction detection, prediction of occult or future atrial fibrillation, valvular heart disease, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, long-term heart-failure prediction, and cardiac amyloidosis remain primarily validation-stage or risk-enrichment applications. Across domains, broader adoption is constrained by label quality, calibration, transportability, operating-threshold selection, and limited patient-outcome evidence. AI-ECG is therefore best positioned as clinician-supervised decision support linked to explicit downstream testing and care pathways.

items.title: True Digital Poiesis: A Conceptual Framework and Interface Design for Generative AI in the Humanities
items.abstract: This article introduces True Digital Poiesis (TDP), a conceptual pedagogical framework and proposed interface design for engaging generative AI in the Humanities. Drawing on experiential learning theory and grounded in the humanistic preoccupation with alterity — the otherness of history — TDP proposes the use of AI to simulate premodern events while foregrounding the active interpretive effort involved in constructing the past. The framework envisions the design of a digital prompt-builder, the Event Cruncher Stylus (ECS), and a structured critical review process, both of which are designed to support student engagement with the complexities of historical construction. In presenting the theoretical foundation, practical applications, and interface design of TDP, this article argues that precise and responsible use of AI in historical simulation — ranging from non-immersive to fully immersive simulative modes — requires a systematic, embodied method for engaging the alterity of the past. As a conceptual proposal grounded in hermeneutic theory and experiential learning research, TDP is presented here as a framework whose empirical evaluation through classroom implementation and outcome assessment is a primary objective of ongoing and future research.

items.title: Trust but Verify: Testing a Framework for AI Interrogation in Nursing Education
items.abstract: Generative AI produces fluent, confident output that is sometimes fabricated. Nursing students increasingly submit work built on sources that do not exist, or that exist and do not support the claims drawn from them. This session reports two semesters of classroom observation testing whether prompt design can address that problem. The hypothesis was that structuring student prompts to require the AI to validate its own sources would improve detection of hallucinated citations. It did not. Across two sections, students who used the structured format caught fabricated citations at the same rate as students given an open prompt. Structure did change something: structured students were substantially more likely to notice that something was wrong, but no more likely than the open-prompt group to finish the check. The session presents both rounds, including the confound identified in the first and removed in the second, and the limits of the observation, among them students who did not use the assigned structure. It also reports an unplanned finding: the AI tool used to review the submissions produced the same category of error it was reviewing for, misattributing a real paper to a fabricated author across multiple students before the error was caught on human review. Attendees will leave with a way to check sources that starts cheap and gets expensive, a clearer view of why you cannot ask the model to check its own work, and a specific account of where student checking breaks down.

items.title: Trust Rhythm in Human and AI Collaboration for Digital Marketing in Nonprofit and Service Organizations
items.abstract: This paper builds a conceptual model that explains how artificial intelligence changes the temporal structure of trust in a brand and defines the threshold beyond which automation erodes trust instead of supporting it. The study applies framework synthesis to peer-reviewed literature published from 2018 onward, supplemented by four earlier works whose definitions and instruments later studies reuse. Antecedents of trust are coded into four operational domains, namely transparency, authenticity, timeliness and human accountability, and converted into six propositions with explicit falsification conditions. A simulation on synthetic parameters tests the internal consistency of the model. Trust under machine mediation depends on three parameters of communication rhythm: frequency, amplitude and predictability. Artificial intelligence raises frequency and predictability because it removes the dependence of regular communication on staff availability. It lowers amplitude because content produced in volume without organizational substance carries no verifiable information. The simulated trust index reaches an interior maximum, after which further automation pushes it below its unautomated level. Disclosure of machine use is not the decisive variable. The decisive variable is whether the audience can read human authorship behind the message. The paper contributes a matrix for allocating marketing tasks between people and machines, indicators for monitoring communication rhythm, and a disclosure rule that reports the configuration of human control rather than the bare fact of technology use. The model is theoretical, its evidence base is concentrated in commercial settings, and the nonprofit case is therefore a boundary condition awaiting longitudinal and experimental testing.

items.title: Trustworthy AI for Sustainable Cities: A Multimodal Orchestration Agent-Based Framework for Civic Compliance
items.abstract: Sustainable municipal resource stewardship requires a harmonized artificial intelligence (AI) architecture that aligns technical performance with human-centered behavioral dynamics. Traditional smart city enforcement frameworks frequently trigger psychological reactance and perceptual failure in noisy, crowded urban spaces. This study presents HARMONY, a socio-technical edge-computing and agent-based framework that integrates localized computer vision (YOLOv8) with Mesa 3.0 agent modeling to promote non-coercive civic compliance in waste disposal. We formally calibrate behavioral constants, including the Politeness Modifier (Lp = 0.98), Gratitude Loop increment (δ = 0.025), and irreducible human defiance floor (ε = 0.12), grounded in self-determination theory, politeness theory, and empirical habit formation models. We also mathematically resolve sensory asymmetry in Hierarchical Orchestration Logic (HOL) by enforcing strictly normalized, bi-directional modality allocation (wv + wa = 1.0) conditioned on acoustic noise (N) and optical reliability (Qv). Across 100-run Monte Carlo simulations, HARMONY achieves a terminal Correct Disposal Rate (CDR) of 87.9% ± 3.3% (95% CI: [87.3%, 88.6%]), outperforming the coercive baseline (57.0% ± 4.9%). A comprehensive six-arm factorial ablation study isolates the distinct contributions of interactional politeness (+30.5% compliance gain), HOL sensory resilience (+1.6% to +21.4% under severe noise), and gratitude habituation (+0.5% to +30.3% sustained retention). Furthermore, population heterogeneity evaluations across diverse civic cohorts confirm robust performance from civic champions to highly resistant populations. Localized edge prototyping demonstrates 18.4 ms inference latency with 94.2% mAP, operating under an Edge-Only Ephemeral Vector Processing (E-EVP) paradigm that guarantees privacy-by-design. These findings demonstrate that cooperative, polite AI stewardship offers a scalable, legally robust, and ethically aligned alternative to punitive urban surveillance.

items.title: Um encontro entre a festa e a ciência: reflexões sobre as expressões da ciência nos Congressos Brasileiros de Agroecologia (CBAs)
items.abstract: In agroecology, scientificity cannot be reduced to conventional academic formats. Rather, it is distributed across pedagogical devices, sociotechnical arrangements, and collective practices that bring academic science and popular knowledge into relation. This article analyzes how knowledge is produced in the Brazilian Congresses of Agroecology (CBAs). More specifically, it describes the pedagogical devices that structure the circulation, validation, and institutionalization of knowledge within the CBAs, while also proposing an analytical framework for locating and interpreting the expressions of science within these devices. Methodologically, the study combines documentary analysis, semi-structured interviews, and a theoretical review grounded in epistemology, critical theory, and science and technology studies. The analysis identified 24 pedagogical devices, understood not as mere organizational supports for the congress, but as effective mediations in the production of agroecological knowledge. Drawing on philosophy of science, the article argues that the CBAs reconfigure the criteria of scientific legitimacy by fostering expanded circuits of translation, experimentation, mutual recognition, and the public circulation of knowledge.

items.abstract: With the burgeoning development of sophisticated artificial intelligence tools, it is of foremost importance for second language educators to integrate these digital learning platforms into their regular classroom settings, as they will help them deliver clearer pedagogical instructions and design more effective learning materials. Concerning the aforesaid background, the researchers undertook this moderate library study to investigate university EFL learners’ perceptions of the use of ChatGPT in the academic writing learning process. In compliance with this major study objective, the researchers employed a thematic analysis approach while reviewing pertinent findings derived from 30 previously published ChatGPT journal articles. With the help of a thematic analysis approach, the researchers could generate more believable, trustworthy, and relatable findings, as it supported us in subsuming the targeted results into relevant themes. The thematically-categorized research results revealed that ChatGPT allowed the enhancement of writing accuracy, proficiency, strategic competence, motivation, confidence, and positive writing dispositions among global university EFL learners.

items.title: Upper limb movement trajectories in virtual reality versus conventional occupational therapy: a within-subject study
items.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used as a complementary approach to conventional occupational therapy (OT), but it remains unclear whether corresponding VR and physical tasks elicit similar spatial movement characteristics. Evaluating these differences is clinically relevant because movement strategies practiced in VR may influence transfer to real-world activities. This study compared hand trajectory length, as a spatial kinematic indicator, between corresponding VR-based and physical OT tasks in participants with upper-limb motor impairments and healthy controls and evaluated the usability of the VR system. In this comparative within-subject study, 39 participants (20 with upper-limb motor impairments and 19 healthy controls) performed three corresponding OT tasks—range-of-motion (ROM) arc, cone stacking, and peg transfer—under both physical and VR conditions. The order of conditions and tasks was counterbalanced using a Latin square design. Task performances were video-recorded and analyzed using a video-based three-dimensional body-tracking system, with wrist coordinates used to calculate trajectory length. Trajectory length was compared between the physical and VR conditions within each group and between groups within each condition. System usability was assessed using the standard 10-item System Usability Scale (SUS). For participants with upper-limb motor impairments, trajectory length did not differ significantly between VR and physical conditions for the ROM arc ( p = .522) or cone task ( p = .294), whereas peg trajectories were significantly longer in VR ( p = .007). In healthy controls, ROM arc trajectory length did not differ between conditions ( p = .381), while cone and peg trajectories were significantly longer in VR (both p < .001). Between-group comparisons showed no significant differences for the ROM arc or cone tasks under either condition, whereas peg trajectory length differed significantly between groups in both VR ( p = .032) and physical conditions ( p < .001). Mean SUS scores were 76.6 ± 16.4 in healthy controls and 65.4 ± 15.2 in participants with upper-limb motor impairments. Corresponding VR and physical OT tasks showed similar trajectory lengths during the relatively constrained ROM arc task, whereas greater differences emerged during tasks requiring more complex or precise object manipulation. These findings suggest that VR may approximate the spatial extent of hand movement for relatively constrained tasks, but trajectory length alone does not establish equivalence of overall movement quality or motor strategy. Lower usability among participants with upper-limb motor impairments further indicates the need for improved interface design, device ergonomics, and interaction methods to support broader clinical implementation.

items.title: User experience and early adoption of an artificial intelligence application: a mixed-methods sentiment analysis of DeepSeek reviews on Google Play
items.abstract: Purpose The rapid emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot applications has transformed digital information access, yet the theoretical understanding of how users evaluate new AI tools during early adoption remains limited. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model and Expectation Confirmation Theory, the study aims to address a conceptual gap regarding mixed sentiment and explore how demographic factors, such as gender, shape user experience during early adoption. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-methods approach was used to analyze 1,000 Google Play Store reviews. Reviews were categorized by sentiment: positive, negative, mixed (both positive and negative statements) or neutral. Gender predictions were also made from usernames to explore demographic differences in sentiment. Findings Of the 1,000 reviews, 487 were mixed reviews (48.7%), 373 were negative reviews (37.3%), 139 were positive reviews (13.9%) and one was neutral (0.1%), indicating that mixed and negative sentiment predominated. Users were mostly satisfied with DeepSeek’s usability and output quality, but criticized its performance and stability issues. Female users gave more negative reviews than male users (p < 0.05). Research limitations/implications The analysis was conducted on a stratified sample of 1,000 “most relevant” Google Play reviews from a short early adoption period, which may not accurately represent later user experiences or experiences on other platforms. Only reviews from phone users were included, and the neutral sentiment category contained too few cases for comparison. Gender inference was based on usernames and reflects predicted rather than self-identified gender. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as indicative of early user perceptions rather than long-term attitudes. Practical implications The findings indicate that infrastructure reliability is the primary determinant of early user satisfaction. Transparent communication about service limitations is recommended prior to large-scale deployment. For policymakers, the equity implications of performance-unstable free AI services warrant attention, particularly for users with limited access to alternatives. Originality/value The mixed-methods analysis of early DeepSeek user reviews, which distinguishes between mixed sentiment and positive and negative feedback, and incorporates a gender-based comparison, provides timely insight into user expectations and challenges during early adoption, supporting the development of more user-centered and stable AI systems.

items.title: Value perceptions and implementation priorities for public PHR adoption in Taiwan: an importance–performance analysis with the Chuchiming Index
items.abstract: Abstract Background Value perceptions of personal health record (PHR) components at the pre-adoption stage remain underexplored, despite their critical role in promoting the adoption of public PHRs. Importance–Performance Analysis (IPA) may have limitations in identifying priority issues due to skewed distributions of evaluations. Objective To quantitatively assess citizens’ value perceptions of public PHR platform components using IPA according to usage experience and to evaluate the utility of the Chuchiming Index (ChI) as a complement to IPA. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among internet-using citizens. After viewing a video introducing an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered extended PHR platform concept, participants rated the importance and acceptance of platform functions and system design and security components. Participants were grouped by their experience using an existing public PHR platform, and quadrant analysis was conducted using IPA, with ChI used to quantify improvement priorities. Stratified IPA analyses were conducted by age and income, which were identified as factors associated with the use of existing public PHR platforms. Results A total of 177 participants were included in the analysis. All components showed high importance and acceptance regardless of usage experience. Among nonusers, medical record display, wearable data integration, and platform integration fell into Quadrant II, all with positive ChI values. Among users, no items fell into Quadrant II; however, platform integration showed a high ChI value. For system design and security, privacy and security assurance showed the highest ChI values in both groups. Stratified analyses showed marked differences in value perceptions by usage experience among older adults and middle-income groups. Conclusion Value perceptions of individual public PHR platform components differed by usage experience and sociodemographic characteristics. Promoting public PHR adoption requires optimizing strategies that encompass platform design, system implementation, and user uptake according to the needs of different population groups. The ChI complements IPA by enhancing the identification and interpretation of priorities, even under ceiling effects common in public service evaluations. These findings contribute to decision-making regarding the design and implementation strategies of public PHR platforms.

items.title: Virtual Reality (VR)-Based Safety Training for Post-Disaster Responders and Workers: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Post-disaster responders and workers operate in hazardous environments that require rapid decision-making, hazard recognition, and effective safety training. Virtual reality (VR) has emerged in recent years as an innovative tool for immersive occupational safety and health education. This scoping review systematically examines peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 on the use of VR for safety training among personnels across a broad range of fields who perform or are trained to perform disaster and emergency response functions. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, five electronic databases (PubMed, ProQuest Central, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and ERIC) were searched, resulting in 2,202 identified articles; 19 of which met the inclusion criteria after screening and eligibility assessments. The reviewed studies suggest that VR-based safety training, which uses fully immersive simulated environments, can improve learner engagement, situational awareness, hazard recognition, decision-making, and confidence in disaster response scenarios. Several studies have reported higher user satisfaction and increased realism compared with traditional instructional methods such as classroom-based instruction or mock drills. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous, with limitations including small sample sizes, technical challenges, limited scenario diversity, and insufficient long-term evaluation of training outcomes. Overall, VR is a promising supplement to traditional safety and health training for post-disaster responders and workers; however, additional longitudinal research and large-scale studies are needed to further evaluate its effectiveness and long-term applicability in various disaster-response settings.
